query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing an atomically thin high-entropy oxide coating on the surface of a refractory high-entropy alloy will suppress oxygen penetration and stabilize the protective oxide scale, thereby improving high-temperature oxygen resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy with a predominantly BCC structure and a composition optimized for structural applications at extreme temperatures, but exhibiting conventional oxidation behavior under high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Deposit an atomically thin, high‐entropy oxide coating on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure at 800 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., laboratory air at 1 atm) for extended periods (e.g., up to 27 hours) to simulate extreme-temperature structural service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A coherent, dense, atomically thin high-entropy oxide layer that forms a continuous protective barrier on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The coating reduces the solubility and diffusivity of oxygen at the surface and suppresses oxygen penetration into the alloy. Similar to strategies used in oxygen defect engineering in CeO2-based systems, the coating stabilizes the protective oxide scale and minimizes further oxidation-induced degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A marked reduction in oxidation-induced weight gain and microstructural degradation compared to the untreated alloy, leading to improved structural integrity and durability under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory HEA exhibits significant oxidation (e.g., thick, potentially spalling oxide scales and element depletion near the surface) under the same 800 °C, air-exposed conditions.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected primarily under moderate extreme conditions (around 800 °C in air). Under temperatures significantly above 900 °C or in more aggressive oxygen-rich environments, the coating may not provide sufficient protection.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement and the long-term adhesion and stability of the ultrathin coating under cyclic or prolonged exposure remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one group with the atomically thin high-entropy oxide coating and one group without (control). Expose both sets to 800 °C in ambient air (1 atm) for 27 hours. Post-exposure, use techniques such as weight gain measurement, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for oxide scale morphology, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for elemental distribution, and X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification.
measurements: Microstructural changes and elemental depletion near the surface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxygen-induced weight gain, exhibit comparable or more severe microstructural degradation (e.g., cracked or spalled oxide scales), or if the oxide scale morphology (thickness, continuity) is similar to that of the untreated control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Oxide scales will form on any alloy that is exposed to a reactive environment at elevated temperature(s). Stable protective scales are desirable for alloys used in structural applications at high temperatures. A scale can be damaged during service, for example, scale cracking and spallation could occur during thermal cycling owing to differences in the values of coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) between scale and substrate. Thus, healing of the scale via the reformation and growth of the protective oxides is another important requirement []. Recent studies have observed pronounced local structural heterogeneities involving distinct surface and bulk domains of HEOs during synthesis and catalysis processes. Instead of the formation of entropy-stabilized single-phase solid solutions, building surface-confined HEO domains provides an alternative to tailor the surface reactivities of ceria via oxygen defect engineering. Here, we demonstrate the feasibility of constructing atomically thin HEO layers on ceria for enhanced catalysis. Neutron diffraction coupled with a pair-distribution function (PDF) analysis enables an atomistic investigation of the HEO–CeO2 interface, which identifies both the intrinsic interstitial oxygen defects in the bulk lattice and the extrinsic oxygen vacancies on the surface of CeO2. The strong covalency of the transition-metal–oxygen bonds facilitates the formation of surface-confined oxygen vacancies, which promotes efficient oxygen activation and replenishment for enhanced CO oxidation capabilities. reading.lever: Deposit an atomically thin, high‐entropy oxide coating to suppress oxygen penetration and stabilize the protective scale.
reading.why: This method, successful on CeO2 for oxygen defect engineering, offers a novel, transferable strategy to enhance high‐temperature oxygen resistance in refractory HEAs.
